author: Carine Medellus; Daria Knurenko
note:
Dear readers,

We, Carine and Daria, are delighted to share with you the 2026 issue of our magazine, and we hope you enjoy reading it as much as we enjoyed working on it.

Our DoubleSpeak experiences have been some of the most transformative in our lives at Penn; from writing about the magazine in college application essays to attending the first meeting at the Kelly Writers House to listening to the DoubleSpeak playlist together, we have formed so many memories and learned of languages and cultures we had not even heard about.

This year’s issue is extremely rich in terms of geographies, languages, ideas, and new features. A number of translations accepted this year were completed this past summer in a literary translation seminar at La Sapienza University in Rome, taught by DoubleSpeak’s faculty editor, Taije Silverman, who was hosted at La Sapienza by Professor Iolanda Plescia. The variety in submissions by students from the seminar has significantly enriched the linguistic representation in our journal; we received translations in languages DoubleSpeak has never previously featured, such as the translation from Uzbek by Manzura Ravshanbekovna Abdirimova and translations from Kazakh by both Fariza Saidybek and Zarina Nurakhunova. We also expanded our range of forms by accepting our first set of riddles, translated from Crimean Tatar by Denis Ferhatović.

Some of these poems unfold through beautiful abstraction, such as Magzhan Zhumabayev’s “Turned Yellow,” translated by Fariza Saidybek. Others, such as Kunwar Narian’s “Shop that Sells Peace,” translated by Apollo Constantine, speak directly to the unrest the world is experiencing today.

Another highlight of the 2026 spring issue is its abundance of Persian translations: "To Have a Mother" by Fereydoon Moshiri, translated by Mahsa Nikomanesh; "The Aghavan Tree" by Amir Houshang Ebtehaj, translated by Elahe Eizadi; "Ghazal 317" by Hafez, translated by Elnaz Zandian, and "We Are All Okay" by Seyed Ali Salehi, translated by Sogand Shenavar. We hope that these fascinating translations allow our readers proximity to the poems’ authors and Iranian heritage, in place of the distance that the American government is attemptings to install.

Lastly, while this year’s issue contains a number of innovations and changes, we would like to think that we as DoubleSpeak staff were at all times guided by the mission that the translators have faced at all times and that was summarized so precisely by Walter Benjamin: to release in our own language that pure language that is under the spell of another, to liberate the language imprisoned in a work in our re-creation of that work.

With this, we’d like to welcome you to the spring 2026 issue of DoubleSpeak and its many beautiful translations, as well as the stirring musing by Mariam El Naggar about the shifting linguistic nature of blessing, in Arabic and English.

Sincerely,
Daria Knurenko and Carine Medellus
Editors-in-Chief

title: Сёстры – тяжесть и нежность...
author: Osip Mandelstam
poem:
Сёстры – тяжесть и нежность, одинаковы ваши приметы.
Медуницы и осы тяжёлую розу сосут.
Человек умирает. Песок остывает согретый,
И вчерашнее солнце на чёрных носилках несут.

Ах, тяжёлые соты и нежные сети!
Легче камень поднять, чем имя твое повторить.
У меня остаётся одна забота на свете:
Золотая забота, как времени бремя избыть.

Словно тёмную воду, я пью помутившийся воздух.
Время вспахано плугом, и роза землёю была.
В медленном водовороте тяжёлые, нежные розы,
Розы тяжесть и нежность в двойные венки заплела!
transpoem:
Sisters – Heavy and Tender by name – the same are your features.
Wasps and wild bees are busy, sucking on a ponderous rose. 
A man is dying. The warm sand cools down on the beaches. 
And yesterday’s sun on the black stretchers moves to repose. 

Ah, the toils are so tender, and the honeycombs – heavy!
It is easier to lift a stone than to repeat your name.
And the worry – the golden worry I am left with:
How to waste out the burden of time – is the last to remain.

I am drinking the nebulous air, like the murky dark water.
Time is turned up by a plow, and this rose has once been earth.
In a whirlpool the roses are circling, so heavy and tender,
That their tenderness weaves with the heaviness into the wreath!
note:
Earlier translations often fell into two categories: mechanical literary renderings or freer adaptations. The debate over Mandelstam’s translation, framed by D.H. Lawrence and Vladimir Nabokov, reflects the classic tension between poetic freedom and literal fidelity. Lawrence’s versions, based on cribs, read more like creative adaptations — capturing mood but reshaping Mandelstam into Lawrence’s own idiom. Nabokov, by contrast, rejected such liberties, demanding near word-for-word exactness even if the result seemed awkward in English. At the heart of this dispute lies a fundamental question: should a translation recreate the poem’s effect in the new language, or preserve its exact structure and meaning?

Modern scholarship suggests that neither extreme fully serves Mandelstam. Lawrence risks distortion; Nabokov risks unreadability. The most successful translators seek a middle path, honoring Mandelstam’s precision while retaining poetic vitality. The translations presented here attempt to follow this middle course, though leaning somewhat closer to Nabokov’s approach. They aim to preserve the sound of Mandelstam’s poetry while closely following the meaning and maintaining structure — including rhyme, meter, and intonation — as faithfully as possible to the originals. This approach contrasts with many earlier versions.
abio:
In 1891 Osip Emilievich Mandelstam was born in Warsaw (then part of the Russian Empire) to a Jewish family. He grew up in St. Petersburg, where he attended the elite Tenishev School, and later continued his studies in Paris and Heidelberg.

As a leading figure of the Acmeist movement, Mandelstam championed clarity, precision, and cultural depth, setting his work apart from the mysticism of Symbolism. His early poetry collections Stone (1913, 1916) and Tristia (1922) established him as one of the foremost Russian poets. His life, however, was overshadowed by Stalinist repression. In 1933, he wrote an poem about the dictator, which soon came to Stalin’s attention. This led to escalating persecutions: he was arrested, exiled, arrested again, and finally died in a transit labor camp near Vladivostok in 1938. He was buried in a mass grave at an unknown location.

Mandelstam’s poetry is rich in classical, biblical, and historical allusions, reflecting his belief in the continuity between past and present. His verse combines musicality, exact imagery, and philosophical meditation, often revolving around memory, mortality, and cultural survival. Even in exile, his later poems embody both despair and defiance, preserving an inner space of freedom against totalitarianism.
tbio:
Valentin Yemelin, born in 1956 in Moscow, Russia, has lived in Norway since 2001.Yemelin graduated from the Leningrad Institute of Technology in 1976 and from Harvard University in 1997. He currently works at the Collaborating Center of the UN Environment Programme.

Yemelin writes poetry in both Russian and English. His translations from English, Russian, German, Swedish, Danish, and Norwegian have appeared in the poetry magazines Interpoezia, The Write Launch (USA), Vyshgorod (Estonia), and Emigrant Lira (Belgium) . His original poems have been published in White Raven and online in the magazines White Mammoth, Bukvitsa and Golden Fleece. He translated Dennis Nurkse’s family saga Voices over Water and, together with Galina Itskovich, published the translated anthologies Female Poetry of America and Narrative Poetry. He is a laureate of the Fourth International Festival of Russian Poetry and Culture in Israel, and the Fifth World Festival of Emigrant Lira. He was also a finalist of the 13th International Festival of Russian Poetry Pushkin in Britain, the Open Baltic Championship of 2015, and the International World Cup of Poetry, in 2017.

title: Mubtalo bo’ldum sanga
author: Alisher Navoi
poem:
Ko‘rgali husnungni zoru mubtalo bo‘ldim sanga,                         
Ne balolig‘ kun edikim, oshno bo‘ldim sanga?!

Har necha dedimki, kun-kundin uzay sendin ko‘ngil,
Vahki, kun-kundin battarroq mubtalo bo‘ldim sanga.
                                                                           
Men qachon dedim vafo qilg‘il manga, zulm aylading,
Sen qachon deding, fido bo‘lg‘il mango, bo‘ldim sanga!
                                                                           
Qay paripaykarg‘a, dersen, telba bo‘lding bu sifat,
Ey paripaykar, ne qilsang qil mango, bo‘ldim sanga!
                                                                           
Ey ko‘ngul, tarki nasihat ayladim — ovvora bo‘l,
Yuz balo yetmaski, men ham bir balo bo‘ldim sanga!
                                                                           
Jomi Jam birla Xizr suyi nasibimdir mudom,
Soqiyo, to tarki joh aylab, gado bo‘ldim sanga.
                                                                           
G‘ussa changidin navoye topmadim ushshoq aro,
To Navoiydek asiru benavo bo‘ldim sanga.
transpoem:
To behold your beauty, I became lovesick, enslaved by you.
What a fateful day it was when I became so close to you!
                                                                           
I told myself with time, my heart would grow distant from you, 
But with each day, I grew more entangled in you.
                                                                           
When I asked you to be faithful, you showed me cruelty.
When you asked for my devotion, I gave myself to you!
                                                                           
One might ask "To what beauty has this madman lost his mind?"
Oh beauty, do as you will—still, I belong to you!
                                                                           
Oh heart, I’ve turned away from wise advice—go and wander!
As if a hundred troubles were not enough, I became a trouble to you.
                                                                           
Jamshid’s cup and Khizr’s fountain were always my companions.
Oh cupbearer, I cast off the world and became a beggar for you.
                                                                           
In the dust of sorrow, no joy did lovers find.                                                             
I, like Navoi, became a captive – a poor prisoner to you.
note:
I am drawn to this poem by Alisher Navoi not only because he is my favourite poet, but also because the theme of the poem appeals to me. It is about a person who is deeply in love with a beautiful but hard-hearted woman who shows him no kindness. Throughout the poem, the poet beautifully describes how forcefully he is becoming devoted to her, despite his efforts to stop it. He uses a mythical figure (Khizr) and mythical object (King Jamshid’s magic cup) to vividly describe his wretchedness.

One of the most challenging phrases to translate was mubtalo bo’ldum (in both the title and first line), because it is an archaic word combination and no longer used by people in my country, so I had to change the translation there several times to preserve the meaning and the strength of the feeling the poet is depicting. Similarly, paripaykar was another archaic word posing difficulty; it suggests a very beautiful woman. At first, I tried “enchantress,” then “fairy,” and “fairy-winged,” but they did not sound right, so I ended up using “beauty.” The word balo, which means “misery, natural disaster,” also required much effort, but after grappling with it, I think I achieved a more accurate translation.
abio:
Alisher Navoi was a famous poet. He was born in 1441 in Herat, now in Afghanistan. He lived during the time of the Timurid Empire. Navoi is known as the father of Turkic literature, writing beautiful poems in the Chagatai Turkic language during a time when most of his contemporaries wrote in Persian.

He worked as a government leader, but he also built schools, libraries, hospitals, and roads. One of his most famous books is Khamsa, which means “Five Treasures,” and comprises five long poems about love, wisdom, and morality. Navoi also wrote about religion, friendship, and how to live a good life. He died in 1501, but his work is still loved and read today. Alisher Navoi’s writing helped shape the culture and language of Central Asia, and he is remembered as a great thinker and poet.
tbio: Manzura Abdirimova is a master’s student in English and Anglo-American Studies at La Sapienza University in Rome. In her childhood, she was interested in literature and wrote poems and short stories. She translated short poems into English with her fellow students at Sapienza University. While pursuing her bachelor’s degree, she also worked as a translator and wrote articles for Xorazm Yoshlari (“Khorezm Youth”), a newspaper in Uzbekistan.

title: A tutti i giovani raccomando
author: Alda Merini
poem:
A tutti i giovani raccomando:
aprite i libri con religione,
non guardateli superficialmente,
perché in essi è racchiuso
il coraggio dei nostri padri.
E richiudeteli con dignità
quando dovete occuparvi di altre cose.
Ma soprattutto amate i poeti.
Essi hanno vangato per voi la terra
per tanti anni, non per costruirvi tombe,
o simulacri, ma altari.
Pensate che potete camminare su di noi
come su dei grandi tappeti
e volare oltre questa triste realtà
quotidiana.
transpoem:
To our youth I say:
open your books with devotion,
and do not merely skim.
The courage of our fathers
lies within.
Close them with dignity
when other matters surface.
Above all, love the poets.
They’ve tilled the earth for you
over many years – not for graves
or idols, but altars.
You may walk upon us,
great flying carpets,
to go beyond this sad
everyday reality.
note:
During Prof. Tajie Silverman's seminar on translation at the University of La Sapienza in Rome, we were asked to translate a poem from our native Language into English. My girlfriend suggested Alda Merini's A tutti i giovani raccomando, and I thought it was perfect: elegant, simple and with a strong meaning behind it. Later, I read about her life story, and it struck me as something incredible, worthy of praise and deep analysis.

The translation was quite simple, but simplicity does not always equal a straightforward process. Translation from Italian into English always requires considerable changes in prosody and lexical content in order to keep the fundamentals of the piece intact. Even free verse must be adapted to better suit the particular English prosody and the semantic charge of poems. That is why I added the enjambement in /The courage of our fathers / lies within. / not present in the original.

The simplicity of the verses and word choices gave me some peculiar problems to resolve. For example, the verse aprite i libri con religione literally means "open your books religiously", which would imply the author is trying to say we should read often and carefully(like a nun's habit). But if we read the next lines, we understand it is necessary to read "religiously" because our father's courage is present in the books. So the meaning shifts from a temporal command to a moral, temperamental command: we should open our books ceremonially and respectfully because inside we will find our father's courage. I think the word "devotion" perfectly encapsulates both the feeling and the command being transmitted.

I omitted the word “pensate" (which means “to think”) from my translation because I found the other possibilities to be quite awkward: they miss the sense of openness and liberty the author is trying to leave us with. /Think you may walk upon us/ or /Know you may walk upon us/ or /Imagine you can walk upon us/ leave out a crucial subtext from the original: we, the readers and receivers of the poet's work, have been allowed to soar beyond this reality using their work. If we use the word "think," then we lose poetic charge; if we use "know," then we are transmitting security, reassurance, which is not what I believe the author wishes to leave us with. Finally, if we use "imagine," we are deviating from the original meaning by suggesting the reader should create a mental image instead of actually carrying out what the poet wants us to accomplish by reading their poetry.

The last word of the poem, "quotidiana"(/ˈkwɔ.ti.ˈdja.na/), means "daily"; I think it is represented faithfully by the idea of an "everyday reality". Of course, with this translation we are shifting the focus from the word "everyday" to the word "reality"; it is possible that this change could leave the reader with a juxtaposition of the real versus the unreal instead of the original image of escaping from the "everyday". Yet I feel the compound "everyday reality" will more than likely transfer the same meaning to most readers, and few will focus on reality, just a hunch.
abio:
Alda Giuseppina Angela Merini (1931 – 2009) was an Italian writer known for her unique style that captured the traumatic experiences of her life. The Second World War stripped Merini of her youth, as her home was bombed and her family struggled to not starve in the following years. In 1947, she was interned in a manicomio, or asylum, due to her manic and depressive episodes. She spent over ten years in mental institutions, suffering greatly due to the mistreatment she and other patients received daily.

Notably, she started writing poems at the age of 15; her striking verses were first published by Spangoletti in his Antologia. Today, she is especially known for her collection entitled Terra Santa, or "Holy Land," in which she remembers the horrors of Italian mental institutions.
tbio:
Gabriele Costarella is a master's student in Anglo-American Studies at La Sapienza University in Rome. Born in Messina, he is a self-taught English literature aficionado who will talk too much if you’re not careful with your questions.

He has worked as an English teacher, translator, and tour guide, and is currently becoming a researcher. He initially approached translation as a way to pay the bills, but it has since become a delight. He enjoys editing and translating works, adding to the great cultural reservoir we call literature.

title: مادر داشتن
author: Fereydoon Moshiri
poem:
مادر داشتن

تاج از فرق فلک برداشتن
جاودان آن تاج بر سر داشتن

در بهشت آرزو ره یافتن
هر نفس شهدی به ساغر داشتن

روز در انواع نعمت ها و ناز
شب بتی چون ماه در بر داشتن

صبح از بام جهان چون آفتاب
روی گیتی را منور داشتن

شامگه چون ماه رویاآفرین 
ناز بر افلاک و اختر داشتن

چون صبا در مزرع سبز فلک
بال در بال کبوتر داشتن

حشمت و جاه سلیمانی یافتن
شوکت و فر سکندر داشتن

تا ابد در اوج قدرت زیستن
ملک هستی را مسخر داشتن

بر تو ارزانی که ما را خوشتر است
لذت یک لحظه مادر داشتن
transpoem:
To remove the crown from the sky’s head
To wear that crown for eternity

To find a way into the heaven of desire
To sip, with each breath, from the depthless bowl of nectar

To be surrounded all day by luxury and abundance
To embrace a moon-like idol at night

To illuminate the face of the universe at dawn,
like sunlight, from the roof of the world

To flirt with the firmament, stars,
at night, like the dream-maker moon

To fly like the east wind, Saba, through the sky’s green meadow,
wing-to-wing with doves

To reach Solomon’s rank and dignity
To possess Alexander’s grandeur and glory

To remain at the peak of power forever
To conquer the realm of existence

I would toss these off to you, simply,
since I am happier to have a mother for a moment.
note:
In the first line, the poet uses the word calvarium to indicate the place from which the sky’s crown is removed. This word has appeared a lot in Persian literature, but it doesn’t have a poetic counterpart in Englis, so I've replaced it with "head."

In the first line, the sky is compared to a green meadow on which Saba is blowing. I used "meadow" because the poet doesn’t mean a land to plant something on, or somewhere meant for domesticated animals, but rather an expanse of land covered in tall grasses that make wavy shapes when the wind blows. The second line offers a comparison between Saba and a bird, and the act of blowing is compared to the flying of birds. The final image presents Saba and the dove flying together while taking each others' wings (passing through the sky’s green meadow) - like two people walking together, taking each other’s hands. I used dove instead of pigeon, which seems more poetic.
abio: Fereydoon Moshiri (1926-2000) was a celebrated Iranian poet.
tbio: Originally from Iran, Mahsa Nikomanesh is a master’s student in English and Anglo-American Studies at La Sapienza University in Rome. She holds a Bachelor’s degree in English translation and has been working in this field for about three years.

title: Майгүлге
author: Mukagali Makatayev
poem:
Қалақтай едің,
Қабіріңде қалақ тұр.
Туғаныңды, өлгеніңді санап құр.
Сенің аңқау құлағыңдай қалқиып,
Қыр басынан қала жаққа қарап тұр.
Қызым менің,
Гүлім менің,
Аяулым!
Жатыр молаң жотасындай қоянның
Құлпытастың құны маған бес тиын,
Бір-ақ таспен қалай жаншып қоярмын?!
Қойман, ботам.
Керегі не көк тастың.
Қыста ақ қар, жазда шалғын шөп бассын.
Өзің келген май айында ақ нөсер,
Ағыл-тегіл бізбен бірге жоқтассын.
Керегі жоқ көк тастың...
Бұлданба, жүрек, бұлданба!
Жиылып досың тұрғанда,
Жиырып сені жентектер,
Жымысқы қайғы-мұң бар ма,
Бұлданба, жүрек, бұлданба!
Қызығы тайып, қызы өлген,
Жалғыз-ақ сен бе бұл маңда?!
Қыс қайтып, жасыл көктемде.
Қызғалдақ өсер қырларда.
Өкініш айтып өткенге,
Бұлданба, жүрек, бұлданба!
Сары алтын дейді сабыр іс,
Тепкілей берме, өкпемді.
Қыз деген құрғыр сағыныш,
Сағынту үшін кеткен-ді.
Бұлданба, жүрек, бұлданба!
transpoem:
You were small as a spade.
Now a spade stands at your grave.
What’s left of you now are the dates
of your birth and your death.
Toward the city your naïve mound
on this hill turns, looking,
as your naïve ears would tilt, listening.
Daughter of mine,
bloom of mine—
Beloved.
Your grave lies soft—a gentle rabbit’s knoll.
A headstone’s worth—five pounds—won’t make you whole.
How could I place you beneath blue stone?
I won’t, my moon, my pretty one.
What’s the need for a stone?
Let winter wrap you soft in snow,
and summer grasses gently grow.
Let the pouring rain of May, the month you came,
fall down like tears and speak your name.
No need for a stone.
Don’t sulk, my heart, don’t sulk.
When friends come by and hold you near,
the cold should shrink away from here.
What stealthy grief still dares to stay?
Don’t sulk, my heart, don’t turn away.
Are you the only one left here
whose joy and daughter have disappeared?
When winter leaves, in green spring,
tulips will blossom on the hills.
Don’t mourn the past, don’t grieve again.
Don’t sulk, my heart, don’t cry in vain.
They call patience pure yellow gold,
so stop stirring up the ache I hold.
A daughter, that curse of bliss,
was born to go, and leave us this.
Don’t sulk, my heart, please, don’t sulk.
note:
The poem I chose was written by Mukagali Makatayev after the death of his 11 year-old daughter - Maigul.

When I first read this poem, I was struck by its progression from childhood innocence to the inevitability of death. The opening phrase, қалақтай едің, carries an affectionate image of smallness, the kind of expression someone might use when remembering a child. Yet within only a few lines, the same word appears again in a completely different sense — as a shovel standing at the grave. That sudden shift from tenderness to finality was what made me so interested in this poem.

The greatest challenge was how to deal with the word Бұлданба, which means “don’t sulk” or “don’t pout.” The tone is gentle, often consoling, but can also carry mild reproach. Rendering such everyday expressions into English is tricky, because their force depends not only on meaning but also on cultural nuance.

One more difficulty came with the closing line: Туғаныңды, өлгеніңді санап құр. It reduces life to a bare equation, as if nothing remains except two dates on a gravestone. I wanted to capture the bluntness of this statement without making it sound too flat in English. My translation — “What’s left of you now are the dates of your birth and your death.” — tries to retain both the bitterness and the sense of futility that the original conveys.

This process reminded me that translation is never just about words, but about choices. In this poem, that truth lies in the fragile span between birth and death, and the haunting feeling that follows the father.
abio: Mukagali Makatayev is one of the greatest poets of the mid-20th century and is often called the “soul of Kazakh poetry”. He is also a renowned translator, and he brought both Shakespeare’s sonnets and Dante’s Divine Comedy into the Kazakh language.
tbio: Zarina Nurakhunova is pursuing her master's degree in English and Anglo-American Studies at La Sapienza University in Rome. Growing up as a bilingual speaker of Kazakh and Russian, she has always had a passion for languages; this passion has led to a bachelor's degree in foreign languages from one of the leading universities in her home country, Kazakhstan, where she gained fluency in English, Turkish, and some knowledge of German and Italian.

title: غزل شماره ۳۱۷
author: Khajeh Shams od Din Moḥammad Ḥafeẓ e Shirazi
poem:
فاش می‌گویم و از گفته خود دلشادم
بنده عشقم و از هر دو جهان آزادم
طایر گلشن قدسم چه دهم شرح فراق
که در این دامگه حادثه چون افتادم
من ملک بودم و فردوس برین جایم بود
آدم آورد در این دیر خراب آبادم
سایه طوبی و دلجویی حور و لب حوض
به هوای سر کوی تو برفت از یادم
نیست بر لوح دلم جز الف قامت دوست
چه کنم حرف دگر یاد نداد استادم
کوکب بخت مرا هیچ منجم نشناخت
یا رب از مادر گیتی به چه طالع زادم
تا شدم حلقه به گوش در میخانه عشق
هر دم آید غمی از نو به مبارک بادم
می خورد خون دلم مردمک دیده سزاست
که چرا دل به جگرگوشه مردم دادم
پاک کن چهره حافظ به سر زلف ز اشک
ور نه این سیل دمادم ببرد بنیادم
transpoem:
Bluntly, with joy for my words, I unveil this truth.
In the chains of love, I’m free from both heaven and earth.
Once, the Garden’s bird, now left with no parting songs,
For how thus I’ve fallen, deep, trapped in these throngs.
Once, an angel I was, in Paradise I dwelled.
By Adam, I’m down in this ruined cloister, expelled.
The Tooba tree’s shade, the angel’s caress, the pool’s hue;
All forgotten, by the mere thought of the path to you.
Save the alef of the beloved’s frame, no letter carves my heart.
What’s to be done? The Teacher taught me just this one part.
Unknown to the oracles were my stars to see.
O Lord, for what fate has Mother World given birth to me?
Ever since I wore the servants’ mark in the tavern of love,
With each breath comes a fresh gift of pain from above.
Well-deserved, my eyes suffer from the wound in my heart;
For I have given to a mother’s dearest, my heart’s every part.
With a lock of your hair, wipe the tears from Hafez’s face.
Or else, this constant flood washes away my entire foundation and base.
note:
There are many paths to choose from when translating poetry, many principles to light the way. What I personally choose is to stay as close to the author as possible, for both the meaning and the form. The translation should inspire the same emotion and evoke the same image as the original text. As Cicero puts it, I translate sense-for-sense. This is an essential approach to Persian poetry in particular, with the layered meanings and the intent behind every word.

Classical Persian thrives on iham, or ambiguity, and polysemy, and Hafez has one of the most complicated and ambiguous poetic languages. The meaning of his ghazals vary from person to person. His words can have vastly different meanings of earthly life or the divine. For example, when he writes about the Beloved, the gender is grammatically neutral in Persian, he can be speaking about a lover, or even God. Here, English, like other gendered languages, forces the translator to choose a pronoun, and, therefore, just one meaning.

The other essential characteristic, this time related to the form of the text, is the rhyme scheme and melody of the poem. The Persian ghazal is built upon rhyme and often features a radif, a recurring word or phrase at the end of every line. Persian offers a limitless supply of rhymes, but for English to force a strict rhyme scheme often results in verse that sounds comic, reducing the sublime mysticism of Hafez to the cadence of a nursery rhyme. The translator must therefore improvise to preserve the poem's dignity, substituting the original’s auditory effect for an internal rhythm or blank verse that mimics the feeling of the meter. For this translation, at first I decided on blank verse, but the result sounded too soulless and mundane, so I did my best with the rhymes and tried to keep the spirit of the poem intact.
abio:
Khajeh Shams-od-Din Moḥammad Ḥafeẓ-e Shirazi (known as Hafez) was born in fourteenth-century Shiraz, a city celebrated for its gardens, wine, and poets. One of the most admired figures in Persian literature, Hafez stands at the center of Persian culture and literary identity. His Divan, a collection of lyric poems, is found in every household and recited in family gatherings and national celebrations, such as Nowruz and Yalda Night.

Hafez lived in a time marked by political instability and that shaped both the subtlety and boldness of his verse. He is the master of the ghazal, a lyric form of six to fifteen couplets bound not by linear argument but by symbolic coherence and emotional unity. Themes of love and wine provide a space for Sufi thought, spiritual yearning, and reflections on the human condition.

The brilliance of Hafez lies in his radical ambiguity. His ghazals revel in earthly delights of wine, beauty, beloved, and gardens, while simultaneously engaging the metaphysical language of Sufi mysticism. Through intricate metaphor, irony, and musical precision, he creates a space where the sensual and the spiritual coexist, where he praises the beauty of the Beloved, laments separation, meditates on the brevity of life, and prods at religious hypocrisy and political authority. His layered poems invite multiple interpretations, allowing each reader to find a personal meaning in the text.

Hafez’s influence extends far beyond his time and place. Western writers such as Goethe and Emerson admired him, and the practice of "fal-e Hafez," a form of bibliomancy using his Divan, remains alive today. His work endures because it continues to speak across cultures and minds to the deepest human longings for beauty, truth, and transcendence.
tbio: Elnaz Zandian

title: Sonetto 24
author: Gaspara Stampa
poem:
Vengan quante fur mai, lingue, & ingegni,
Quanti fur stili in prosa, e quanti in versi,
E quanti in tempi, e paesi diversi
Spirti di riverenza, e d’honor degni.

Non fia mai, che descrivan l’ire e sdegni,
Le noie, e i danni, che’n Amor soffersi,
Perche nel vero tanti, e tali fersi,
Che passan tutti gli amorosi segni.

E non fia anche alcun, che possa dire,
Anzi adombrar la schiera de’ diletti,
Ch’Amor, la sua mercè, mi fà sentire.

Voi, ch’ad amar per gratia sete eletti,
Non vi dolete dunque di patire,
Perche i martir d’Amor son benedetti.
transpoem:
Come every tongue, all minds that ever thought,
all hallowed styles in prose, all those in verse
and come from every time, and lands diverse,
those spirits who have read, and rhymed, and taught.

They’ll never write the scorn, the glances dark
that I have felt in love – its loss and spurn,
which all so grave and manifold did turn
they’re worse by far than passion’s usual mark.

And no, no one could ever come reveal
or sketch all those delights, in endless lines,
that Love, when he has willed, has made me feel.

You, whom grace has called to lovers’ eyes,
be unashamed, be unafraid of pain:
the saints of love will all be canonised.
note:
Stampa’s sonnet reads to present-day Italian ears as a combination of the utmost concentration of meaning with surprising linguistic ease. Though the language is, overall, unmistakably archaic, the rhyme scheme sounds as rhythmic as a bell, often punctuating words that feel simple and current; they read like logical keywords of a poetic manifesto.

The text grounds a declaration of artistic mastery in the exceptionality of its object – of the experience of love that the entire collection aims to portray. The first quatrain opens onto the limitless horizons of a literary canon past, present, and future (possibly multilingual: paesi diversi, or "lands diverse"), only to be met with the second quatrain’s denial that anyone else but Stampa could write about what she is describing. It is a love exceeding the Petrarchan referential frame both in pain and in pleasure(as the first tercet reveals). The poetic voice implicitly invokes the most current poetic tradition, and though respecting its form(and partly its lexicon), it uses it to declare its own creative overcoming of it.

All the aspects I mentioned earlier are encapsulated in the extraordinary verse Non vi dolete dunque di patire: Stampa uses two near-synonyms, which both mean to suffer (dolersi, patire), to say (in Jane Tylus’s masterful 2010 translation): "don’t ever regret that you suffer so." The love-pains so central in Petrarchan poetry are here compared to the physical pain of the legendarily gruesome deaths of Catholic saints, not just to achieve a conceit that rewrites Petrarchan topoi into a Baroque conceit, reminiscent of John Donne, on the deeply physical nature of love’s anguish, but also vindicating its dignity. As the first sonnet in the collection suggests, the canonisation of these saints might come from the achievement of being able to write exceptional poetry: art as the crowning glory of life.
abio:
Gaspara Stampa (~1523-1554) was a poet. Historical sources describe her as a talented singer and musician. Though only a handful of her poems were published during her lifetime, her Canzoniere, a collection of 310 sonnets, was given to the press by her sister Cassandra in 1554, six months after Gaspara’s death.

Gaspara Stampa’s artistic activity intersects with wider trends of the Italian XVI century – an emerging tradition of women writing poetry, as well as a much wider movement of intellectuals engaging with the Petrarchan tradition. Francesco Petrarca had founded a poetic sensibility based on a rich, often spiritualised meditation on the experience of love; the dominant move in XVI-century Italian poetry was precisely a rewriting of Petrarch, whose legacy was creatively spun by each poet into different individual threads.

Stampa’s intervention in the movement has long been read as unconventionally centered on physical, tormented love. After almost two hundred years of relative oblivion, her collection was rediscovered in 1738 and re-edited in the light of a largely biographical interpretation – as the faithful record of her relationship with Count Collaltino da Collalto. More recent critical trends have attempted to overcome a purely biographical reading, underlining instead the intellectual dimension of her engagement with Petrarch’s legacy and contemporary culture.
tbio: Giulia Drago is a PhD student in English linguistics at La Sapienza University in Rome. She is currently studying early modern ideas about language from the vantage point of rogue books: Renaissance guides to the (possibly imaginary) secret language of thieves and tricksters.

title: 月宫新詩經四章
transtitle: Four Stanzas of New Shijing on the Moon Palace
author: Shi Yan
poem:
昨天余到月宫影戲浣看戲，時正四點二刻，一到裏面，坐位老早满了，幸而遇若一個招待生，指引我一個坐位，當時尚未開影，我偶然回頭一看，［余不是吊邦子因孤坐無聊耳］所見的多是一雙雙一對對的悄人，或未婚的夫婦或己婚的夫妻，交頭接耳，喁喁唧唧的不知講的甚麼說話，個中風味，真是令人艶羡的很啊，若使我有順風耳千里眼的本事，那末恐怕有一打的新聞報，都不能登我的新聞哩，我回到家裏無事偶作新詩經四章，以搏䦧月宫諸君莞爾一笑耳。 
 
喁喁細語交頭接耳
  語者伊誰  一男一
女  
 
喁喁細語乍吐乍止
匪歌拍指  恐垣有
耳  
 
喁喁細語  何其多
矣匪為多矣情之濃
矣喁喁細語  情旣
濃矣我愛爾爾我愛
爾爾
transpoem:
Yesterday I went to the Moon Palace Cinema to see a movie. It was exactly 4:30. As soon as I entered, the seats had long since been filled. Luckily I found an usher, who pointed me to a seat. At that time the movie hadn’t yet started. As soon as I turned my head (I wasn’t looking to flirt, it’s just boring to sit by oneself) I saw: quiet people in pairs, unmarried young folk, married couples, whispering in each others’ ears, whispering sweet nothings that could not be overheard. Being in the midst of this was enough to make someone quite jealous. Even if I had exceptionally good hearing and vision, I’m afraid no newspapers would print this news. I returned home and with nothing to do, happened to write the below “New Shijing” poem in four stanzas, in order to win the smiles of the group at the Moon Palace Cinema. 

[Couples] speaking in soft low tones 
Whispering in each others’ ears 
Who is speaking? 
One man, one woman 
 
[Couples] speaking in soft low tones 
First speaking, then falling silent 
Tapping fingers to the melody 
Afraid the walls have ears 
 
Whispering 
How could there be so much? 
There is so much 
The passion is thick 
 
Whispers 
The passion is thick 
I love er er 
I love er er
note:
I chose this poem because it came with this remarkable explanatory note; usually, these New Shijing poems don’t have something so helpful for our interpretation. It helps paint the picture of a crowded Shanghai cinema where lovers can have privacy and entertainment away from the rest of society. Love in the public space was part of the radical cultural change China was experiencing in the 1920s, and it was evidently a selling point for this cinema.

One difficulty I’ve had with translating Chinese poems is that the meaning can often seem very obvious, but rendering it in poetic English is quite challenging. Chinese poetry is terse, uses archaic vocabulary, and says a lot with a little.
abio: The poet Shi Yan was not anyone famous or noteworthy, and there is no further information on his identity. It is likely he was writing under a pseudonym. "The Moon Palace Cinema" was part of a larger group of entertainment buildings in Shanghai in the late 1920s, including a Moon Palace dance hall. This poem was likely written as an advertisement for the atmosphere on offer, there.
tbio: Eric Wang is a senior at the University of Pennsylvania studying English. He grew up in Lansdale, Pennsylvania and speaks English and Mandarin Chinese. His interest in the classical worlds of Greece and Rome, as well as history, inform his translation of this poem, which adapts a classic form of Chinese poetry to the modern age of newspapers and advertisements. For this translation and interpretation, Eric was assisted by his advisor, Professor Chloe Estep, in the Department of East Asian Languages and Civilizations.

title: 我曾今敞开的，还没有关闭
transtitle: What I Threw Wide Open Once, Still Has Not Closed
author: Yu XiuHua
poem:
我不想让玫瑰再开一次,不想让你再来一遍
风不停地吹,春天消逝得快,又是初夏了
吹过我村庄的风吹过你的城市
流过我村庄的河流流过你的城市
但是多么幸运,折断过我的哀伤没有折断过你

偶尔,想起你。比如这个傍晚
我在厨房吃一碗冷饭的时候,莫名想起了你
刹那泪如雨下。
这无法回还的生疏是不能让我疼的
再不相见就各自死去也不能让我疼啊
陌生的人间,这孤独也不能叫我疼了

真是说不出来还有什么好悲伤
浩荡的春光里,我把倒影留下了
把蛊惑和赞美一并举起了
生命之扣也被我反复打过死结
然后用了整个过程,慢慢地,慢慢松开

但是这个世界你我依旧共存
还是一件不可思议的事情
transpoem:
I don’t want the roses to bloom once more, don’t want you to return.
The wind keeps blowing, the spring quickly vanishes, again it is summer.
The wind that has swept across my village has swept across your city;
The river that has flowed past my village has flowed past your city;
But how fortunate, the grief that has broken me has not broken you.

Miss you, sometimes. Like this evening
When I was eating a cold meal in the kitchen, I thought of you.
In a split second the tears rain down my face.
That our distance is immutable cannot give me pain;
That, if we never cross paths again, then we’d go die our own little deaths, 
cannot give me pain either;
In this strange mortal coexistence, 
even this loneliness cannot pain me.

Honestly, can’t really say what there is left to grieve over.
In the infinity of spring, I leave behind my reflection
And raise up my praise, and delusion.
I’ve tied the knot of life in dead-knots over and again
And then after the entire process, I have slowly, slowly untied it.

But that, in this world you & I coexist still,
That is still a miraculous thing.
note: Chinese poetry, both ancient and modern, is characterized by a higher tolerance for vagueness that romance languages do not have as much of. Some of this tolerance is translated here, as seen in certain absences of personal pronouns. I have also elected not to explain some terms, such as the “dead-knot,” in my approach to retain some of the foreign aspects that come from reading a translation.
abio: Yu Xiuhua is a Chinese poet from Hengdian village in Hubei, China. She has cerebral palsy and writes about themes of love, disability, truth, place and death. She rose in popularity in 2014 through online media and the Chinese literary magazine Poem.
tbio: Michelle Zhang is a student at the University of Pennsylvania double majoring in Classics and Philosophy, Politics, and Economics. She grew up in Shanghai and writes poetry, prose, and essays.

title: 5. Лірична химера
author: Attila Mohylyny
poem:
Коли надходить час іти коханим,
то тільки музика, як передчуття вокзалу
принесе спогад про золотаві плечі жінки,
що на тлі білих ковдр
були тільки як сонячний відблиск
на речах, залишених у кімнаті.

Ми прощаємось трохи сумно біля входу
в метро,
і наш подих розтає в морозному повітрі,
незграбний, як міф про вічне кохання.
І тільки коли наші очі зустрічаються,
ми посміхаємось легко і просто,
і ця посмішка,
ніби вогники цигарок вночі,
вихоплює з темряви наші обличчя,
і раптовий спалах очей,
і розуміння того,
що наше прощання —
світле, як музика полину
край шатра,
край сонця мандрівного.
transpoem:
When the time comes for lovers to part,
only music, as if a foretelling of a train station,
will bring memories of the women’s gilded shoulders
which, contrasting with the white rugs on the wall,
were only a sunglint
resting on rooms and things.

We are saying our farewells, somewhat sadly, by the subway entrance,
and our breath melts into the frosty air,
awkward, like the myth of eternal love.
And only when our eyes finally meet
do we smile lightly, easily,
and these smiles,
like a lit cigarette at night,
bring our faces out of darkness,
with the sudden spark in our eyes,
and the understanding that
our farewell is
bright like the music of pollen
beside a hut,
in the wandering sun.
note:
Translating a part of Mohylyny’s cycle “Chimeras,” which consists of seven parts — Unintelligible Dreaming, On a Murky Street, Chimeric Spring, Patriotic Chimera, Lyrical Chimera, Industrial Chimera, and Naked Chimera — was something I decided to do because of the unparalleled lightness I found in each part.

The images Mohylyny creates are warm yet fraying and ephemeral, like the old white rug on the wall mentioned in the poem. At the same time, the grammar he chooses is loose and flowing as well — mostly thanks to the enjambments, such as “bright like the music of pollen/beside a hut,/ in the wandering sun.” The two images he creates here of the music of pollen, first by a hut and then in the wandering sun, are unexpected and vivid both on their own and as seen in relation to each other, but the enjambment highlights the individuality of each.

Together, its small but memorable images and unbothered grammar contribute to the elusiveness of the poem as a whole.

Another interesting aspect of this poem is its title, "Lyrical Chimera"; It’s quite obscure in the sense that it leaves much room for interpretation, but it is also undeniably warm and welcoming, setting the scene for the rest of the poem and how filled with unexpected, momentary smiles it is.
abio: Attyla Mohylyny is a Ukrainian poet writing in the 20th century. His most famous poetry collection is called "Kyiv Contours", and it’s also where I found this poem that caught my attention. Referred to as the “urbanist of his generation”, he is well-known for his refreshing and undeniably modernist depiction of Ukrainian urban spaces in his poetry. Mohylyny’s poetic language is a blend of intimate understanding and gentle noticing.
tbio: Daria Knurenko is a sophomore at the University of Pennsylvania studying Comparative Literature and History of Art. She grew up in Chernihiv, Ukraine, and speaks Ukrainian, English, French, German, and Russian. She translates from and into English, French, Ukrainian, and Russian, focusing on nineteenth and twentieth century poetry. She is the Editor-in-Chief of DoubleSpeak this year. Having lived in different countries has informed her interest in the ways people communicate across languages and cultures, as well as literary translation, which brings these notions together.

title: Сарғайдым
author: Magzhan Zhumabayev
poem:
Сарғайдым күннен күнге қуат кеміп, 
Қалың ой - қара жылан жүректі еміп. 
Ақырын бітіп барам жанған шамдай, 
Көзіме ыстық жастар мөлт-мөлт келіп. 
Апырм-ай, ауыр болды-ау күнді өткізу, 
У жұтып, айдан ұзын түнді өткізу!- 
Қозғалып, сөйлеп, ойнап, тірі жатып, Өлем 
деп жас өмірден күдер үзу. 
Соғасың жиі-жиі, жүрек, неге? 
Соққанмен жандана ма солған дене? Сары 
су денені улайд тамырларда, Тазарып, 
енді оны қан етем деме. 
Қалмады көздің нұры, көрге айналдым, 
Қараны - ақ, ақты - қара дерге айналдым. 
Дямадай пісіп тұрған екі бетім 
Қуарып, қаны қашып, күлге айналдым. 
Жайылды бар денеме уы дерттің, 
Мінекей, екі ай болды жалын жұттым. Күндіз 
- Күн, түнде күміс Ай көрмеймін, Дариға, 
жаным - азат, денем - тұтқын. 
Барады күннен күнге азап асып, 
Өлім тұр анадайда қойнын ашып, 
«Қинала түссін əлі!»- дегендей-ақ, Аяғын, 
күлімсіреп, санап басып. 
Жасаған! Тез алатын ажал жоқ па? 
Қинама, тез өлейін, ұшыр оққа. Шыжылдап 
дене, шырқырап жан берейін, Жалыны 
көкке шыққан түсір отқа!
transpoem:
I turned yellow — day by day, my strength dissolves,
Knotted thoughts — like vipers
Siphoning the blood from my heart.
I’m burning out, a candle reaching its end,
As warm tears fall — I let them freely flow.
Oh, how long the days, how bitter and unkind,
The nights — like poison poured into my mind.
I breathe, I move, I speak, I laugh in pain,
And yet I know — I’ll never live again.
Why do you beat and beat, heart of mine?
A ruined body will not rise with time.
This yellowish slush fills my veins, not blood —
Don’t speak of healing — It’s far too late for that.
The light in my eyes has turned to stone,
Black seems like white, and white has turned to clay.
My cheeks, once flushed like fruit in summer sun,
Have paled to ash — their ripeness all undone.
This pain soaked through me, limb to aching limb,
Two months I’ve burned in silence, raw and dim.
By day I see no Sun, by night no Moon.
My soul longs for release, but my body in chains.
The torment grows — it boils, it will not cease,
And Death stands near me, arms spread in embrace.
“Let him suffer more!” it seems to say,
It smiles, and counts its steps across the floor.
Creator! Is there no swift death for me?
Strike now — don’t let me suffer endlessly.
Let body sizzle, let the soul cry loud,
Throw me into fire and let the flame
Rise to the sky!
note:
When I first encountered Сарғайдым, I was struck by its raw honesty and emotional intensity. Magzhan Zhumabayev’s voice feels painfully human, balancing resignation with a fierce desire for freedom. The title itself, literally “I turned yellow,” is deeply symbolic: in Kazakh, "yellowing" suggests withering, fading, and losing vitality, much like autumn leaves. It resonated with me as a powerful image of a person drained by suffering and time.

Translating this poem challenged me on several levels. First, the musicality of Kazakh is very different from English. Kazakh poetry often uses repeated sounds, internal rhymes, and a steady rhythm of syllables that can be hard to echo in English without sounding forced. I tried to prioritize the emotional flow and vivid imagery rather than duplicate the rhyme, believing the core spirit was more important than exact metrics.

Second, some cultural metaphors were difficult to carry over. For instance, the line “Black seems like white, and white has turned to clay” reflects a world where truth is twisted under repression. In Kazakh, this imagery felt to me like a subtle protest against forced confessions and a system where nothing is as it should be. I wanted to preserve that suggestion without overexplaining it.

I was drawn to this poem because it felt timeless: a portrait of hopelessness, but also a cry for spiritual dignity. Translating it was an act of solidarity — bringing one man’s voice from a century ago into a new language, where its emotional truth could still matter.
abio:
Magzhan Zhumabayev was a Kazakh poet, educator, translator and thinker whose work defended Kazakh language and culture under Russian imperial rule and Soviet repression. As a leader of the Alash movement for national autonomy and educational reform, he was arrested in 1929 on fabricated charges of nationalism and espionage, then sent to a harsh labor camp in Northern Russia, where he suffered severe illness and exhaustion. His wife, Zuleikha, risked everything to preserve his manuscripts and support him. Although freed briefly in 1936 thanks to literary advocates, he was rearrested in 1937 and executed during Stalin’s Great Purge.

Zhumabayev’s poetry contains both romantic themes — praising love, nature, motherland and beauty — and a deeply philosophical, symbolist vision that seeks freedom beyond the harsh realities of his era. Through vivid imagery and moral reflection, his work offers spiritual strength and quiet resistance. Banned for decades, his poems survived thanks to Zuleikha’s courage and were only published after Kazakhstan’s independence in 1991. Today, Zhumabayev is honored for his lyrical honesty and universal vision of freedom, making him one of Kazakhstan’s most important literary voices.
tbio: Fariza Saidybek was born and raised in Kazakhstan, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in Translation Studies and gained experience with legal translation as well as freelance interpreting for business events. Now pursuing a master’s degree in English and Anglo-American Studies at La Sapienza University in Rome, she has become drawn to the quiet power of literature and creative translation. She is fascinated by the ability of words to cross borders like travelers, picking up traces of each place they pass through. She loves how reading poetry in a second language can feel like seeing the same sunrise from a new hill. She hopes to keep exploring how meaning and culture shift and grow.

title: Sole d'ottobre
author: Ada Negri
poem:
Godi. Non hai nella memoria un giorno
più bello, un giorno senza nube, come
questo. E forse più mai ne sorgerà
un altro così bello, pe’ tuoi occhi.
Se pur l’ultimo fosse di tua vita
– l’ultimo, donna -
, sii contenta: rendine
grazie al destino.

                      È così pura questa
gioia fatta di luce e d’aria: questa
serenità ch’è d’ogni cosa intorno
a te, d’ogni pensiero entro di te:
quest’armonia dell’anima col punto
del tempo e con l’amor che il tempo guida.
Non più grano né frutti ha ormai la terra
da offrire. Sta limpido l’autunno
sul riposo dell’anno e sul riposo
della tua vita. Il fisso azzurro, immemore
di tuoni e lampi, stende il suo gran velo
di pace sulle rosseggianti chiome
delle foreste; e il sole il cuor t’accende
come fa con le foglie che non sanno
d’esser presso a morire. E tu – che sai –
tu non temi la morte. Ora che il grembo
non dà più figli, e quelli che ti nacquero
a’ tuoi begli anni già son fatti esperti
del mondo e van per loro audaci vie,
che t’importa morir? Quand’è falciata
la spiga, spoglia la pannocchia, rosso
il vin nei tini, e le dorate noci
chiaman l’abbacchio, e fuor del riccio scoppia
la castagna, che importa la minaccia
dell’inverno, alla terra?…

                                             O veramente
tuo questo tempo, donna: o tua compiuta
ricchezza! O, fra due vite, la caduca
e l’eterna, per te libera sosta
di grazia! Godi, fin che t’è concessa.
Non sei più corpo: non sei più travaglio:
solo sei luce: trasparente luce
d’ottobre, al cui tepor nulla matura
perché già tutto maturò: chiarezza
che della terra fa cosa di cielo.
transpoem:
Rejoice. In your memory, you have no day
more bright, no day more cloudless, than
this. And perhaps never again will a day rise as fair
before your eyes.
Even if it were the last of your life
— the last, oh woman -, be content: give thanks 
to fate for it.

                       So pure is this
joy made of light and air: this
serenity that is all around
you, and in every thought within you:
this harmony of the soul with the point
of time and with the love that time guides.
The earth has no more grain or fruit
to offer. The autumn lies limpid
upon the year’s repose and the repose
of your own life. The steadfast blue, forgetful
of thunder and lightning, lays its great veil
of peace over the reddening crowns
of the forests; and the sun kindles your heart
as it does the leaves that do not know
they are about to die. And you, who know,
do not fear death. Now that the womb
bears no more children, and those born from you
in your young years know
the world and go their bold ways, what need do
you have to fear death? When the wheat is
reaped, the cob stripped, the wine glows red
in the vats, and the golden walnuts
call the thrush, and the chestnut bursts from its
burr, what matters the menace
of winter, to the earth?...

                                                   Oh truly
yours is this time, woman: yours, oh your fulfilled
wealth! Oh, between two lives, the mortal
and the eternal, a free pause of grace is granted
you. Rejoice, until you can.
You are no longer body: you are no longer labour:
you are only light: transparent October light,
to whose warmth nothing ripens
as everything is already ripe: clarity
that from the earth makes a thing of heaven.
note:
Translating this poem was challenging both stylistically and linguistically because of the elevated and old-fashioned tone of the original twentieth century Italian. In my translation, I aimed to reproduce as closely as possible the original solemn and old-sounding lexicon, for example by choosing “repose” instead of “rest,” “rejoice” instead of “enjoy,” and “limpid” instead of “clear,” given that all these pairs are semantically close but the former terms reflect more the spiritual and meditative tone of the original. Additionally, one particularly tricky sentence was rendine grazie al destino. While “be grateful for your fate” would have conveyed the message just as well, I decided to translate it with “give thanks to fate for it” to preserve its prayer-like quality.

Another challenge lay in retaining the dense network of metaphors that compare an elderly women to the autumnal landscape (through “repeat wheat,” “stripped cob,” and “fruitless earth,” for example). Throughout the text, natural and human cycles are constantly symbolically intertwined. Therefore, it was essential to preserve this correspondence without flattening its symbolic richness, so in these instances I took care to find exact equivalence between the Italian and the natural English terms (for example, with “purr,” “crowns,” and “thrush”). Sometimes, lexical ambiguity was also crucial to retain. A particularly complex example is the noun travaglio which can mean both “toil” but also “labour,” in the obstetric sense. In the final version of the translation, I chose “labour” to keep this double resonance: both the pain of physical work and the creational suffering of motherhood.

The most critical areas were syntax and rhythm, which are fundamental features of a poem and ones, I believe, that need to be preserved. Italian allows for implicit subjects, longer sentences and greater verb dislocation, whereas English is not as syntactically flexible. Adapting the intricate Italian phrasing into the more linear English structure was therefore one of the main difficulties, which I tried to carry out to the best of my abilities.
abio:
Ada Negri was an Italian poet who lived between 1870 and 1945. She was born in Lodi into a working class family and became the founder of the Female National Union. October Sun is taken from her poetry collection Il Dono (The Gift), one of her later works, published in 1936, in which she confronts death and reflects on her own life, defining it as a gift. This expression of gratitude is the final culmination of her gradual turn towards faith and her eventual attainment of profound serenity.

Today, she is recognised as a major literary figure who made art out of women’s everyday experiences in a society where their voices were still mostly unheard. However, back in the day, the reception of her poetry was mixed: Benedetto Croce, an important literary critic, criticised her for her melodiousness and readiness of emotions that, he misogynistically argued, constituted a “feminine flaw” that could only lead to imperfect art. Conversely, Vincenzo Schilirò, a lesser-known critic, thought of her work as incredibly successful in terms of capturing and artistically engaging with the toils of a generation.
tbio: Manuel Rumiano is a master’s student in English and Anglo-American Studies at La Sapienza University in Rome. He earned his bachelor’s degree in Modern Languages in 2024 from the same institution and is fluent in Italian, English, French and Spanish. Rumiano currently works as an editor for Transitions, a postgraduate journal, and he contributes to Mapping Resistance, a translation project in collaboration with Northwestern University, which focuses on WWII memoirs. He is interested in translation studies and English linguistics.

author: Mariam ElNaggar
note:
Someone sneezes in the office on Park Avenue in the middle of June. It's my first real summer in New York, the junior-to-senior-year internship I had been waiting for. The room of analysts speaks the answer in unison—Bless you. Bless you. Bless you.

I don't.

The silence that follows is small but heavy, like a coin placed on my desk. It doesn't accuse. It just sits there, catching the light, waiting to be picked up. By the third office sneeze that week, I begin to say it back. Quick, polite, bloodless. The air closes neatly over where I'd been silent.

Under the fluorescent lights of the building, even language feels like dress code. Neutral colors. No perfume. “Bless you,” as a kind of company policy—something everyone does without thinking, the same way everyone hovers outside conference rooms until the calendar confirms the room is theirs. I copy: how to laugh at jokes I don't find funny. How to say “I'm good, how are you?” in the elevator, then step out before anyone answers. How to eat lunch alone without looking lonely.

At home, in the satellite city west of Cairo where I grew up, a response to a sneeze is not ornamental. It's a call. The sneezer speaks first and someone always answers.

Al-hamdulillah (praise be to God) is what I say after I sneeze. It's a word with many lives. We say it after relief and after loss, when we stand up from a fall, when a phone call ends better than we feared. We say it for food and survival and for the fact of still being here. I cannot list all the moments to which it belongs.

The room replies: yarhamkom Allah. May God have mercy on you.

Then it's my turn again: yarhamna w yarhamkom. May He have mercy on us and on you. Mercy here moves in a circle. It requires another body. Another voice. I am inside the us it creates.


The Arabic word for mercy, rahmah, is the same one we use when someone passes. It's also the word I return to during Ramadan, the month of fasting and nightly prayer, when forgiveness becomes something you practice whether or not you can point to a specific sin.

In that month, prayer slows the day down enough to examine it. I ask to be forgiven not for one clear transgression, but for the accumulation of small failures that don’t announce themselves—for the moment I looked away, for the kindness I felt but didn’t act on. Rahmah makes room for mercy that doesn’t exile you for being unfinished.

In different families, and in different countries and villages inside the same country, the responses to a sneezer's al-hamdulillah vary like dialects of love. They travel by ear, by repetition. You borrow one, keep it, and eventually it belongs to you.

My mother, who believes in routine the way other people believe in luck, answers to yarhamak Allah with ghafar Allah lana w lakom. May He forgive us and you. Her mercy moves toward repair, toward balance, as if forgiveness is something you keep practicing so it doesn’t slip.

My grandfather Gedo Samir, the family's center of gravity, changes the rhythm a little. Instead of closing the exchange with the familiar yarhamna w yarhamkom (may He have mercy on us and on you), he says yahdeena w yahdeekom. May He guide us and guide you. His version turns mercy into direction, as if the kindest thing God can give is a path.

My grandmother Sousou sits at the head of the room in her armchair, her hands folded, the hum of conversation rising and falling around her. She doesn’t move much anymore. When someone says al-hamdulillah, she answers from where she is: yarhamkom Allah w yahdeekom. May God have mercy on you and guide you. The response to that—yahdeekom Allah w yusliḥ balek, may God guide you and ease your mind—returns the blessing gently, without widening it. There is no “us” in her conclusion. Her mercy rests exactly where it’s placed.

Each phrase carries a kind of surrender. Mercy as breath returning to the body after being held too long. We say these words asking that God loosen what clenches the heart. It's mercy that gathers us, folds us back into the world, says: you are still here, you are still held.

I think about what “mercy” means in English, and I realize I rarely hear the word at all. When I do, it belongs to institutions—courts, churches, battlefields. A merciful verdict. An act of mercy. It's something the powerful extend downward, something you plead for when you've run out of options. Even its gentlest uses carry the weight of judgment. But rahmah is immediate. It's in the kitchen, in the car, in the moments between leaving and staying.

Here, in the U.S., words land on drywall and stop. They don’t wait for an answer.

After a few weeks of Manhattan heat and the overcorrecting air-conditioning of Midtown in July, I can say "bless you" without thinking. No one looks up. I tuck the coin of silence into a drawer and keep typing. I have learned the sound of this new form of belonging—small, clean, dissolving.

On the F train in the mornings, my body learns new rhythms. I stand as if my knees were built for this small sway. The people around me hold their empty coffee cups like talismans. Someone sneezes. “Bless you,” a stranger says, eyes on the door. The train takes a corner like it's remembering how. I raise my hand to my face, feel the familiar lift in my chest that says now, and hold it until the feeling passes. Sometimes even the body misreads its own instructions. I think about what else I've trained myself not to say.

A rhythm is a way of staying. A rhythm is also a way of leaving without anyone noticing.

My uncle, my mom's brother, used to say a healthy body thanks God by expelling what doesn't belong. He loved riddles and stray facts, the kind that made you stop chewing just to listen. He gave me my first real books and could make me laugh until I forgot to be shy.

The Prophet loved the sneeze, he’d remind me, because it brings relief. I was eleven or twelve then, still in my stiff school uniform, before I’d learned how to roll the sleeves or knot the belt. Back then I believed everything had a place—dust on the sill, cumin on the air, grief traveling in straight lines between people who spoke to one another in the same words.

Silence becomes a kind of fluency. Especially around certain words. On campus, in the news, online—some language is watched more closely than others, flattened as soon as it leaves your mouth. It feels both dangerous and indulgent to speak. Dangerous because words can cost more than you intend. Indulgent because silence, too, has a cost, and I am protected enough to afford it. I come from a place of conflict, but not from its most exposed edge.

In the kitchen of my office in Manhattan, the news plays without sound, captions molding themselves into safe shapes. Crisis. Casualties. Complicated. The words smooth the edges until the screen looks like weather. I drink my coffee, stand for half a breath, and learn to step away at the right time. Belonging, I am learning, has as much to do with manners as with belief.

At night, I walk back to the apartment in Midtown, along the blocks that have started to recognize me. The bodega on the corner keeps the bell that chimes too loudly. The man there calls everyone “boss.” Somehow it works as a blessing. I buy bread I will forget to eat and leave with a “take care” that rings truer than most prayers here. I am not sure what to do with the small kindness of the ordinary when the world is on fire on mute.

When I fly home before senior year, my internship over, Egypt is still on the list of countries being considered for Trump's travel ban. My American friends think I'm reckless for going, but I tell them I'd rather risk not getting back into the U.S. than stay away from Egypt a day longer.

Past the airport doors, the air is the same as always: hot, unbothered, certain of itself. It isn't a clean smell. It isn't meant to be. West of Cairo, my house sits beside my grandfather's, my uncle's, my aunt's—one family stitched into the same patch of dust.


My mother waits in the living room that always smells of oud and sandalwood. She's sitting with the window behind her—the one that looks out onto the moonlit garden and makes the room glow unevenly, half-shadow, half-silver. She sees me first. The smile arrives before she lets it.

Ezayak? How are you.

Alhamdulillah.

The words settle, closing the space between us more surely than my steps ever could. Her face registers the distance at my edges like a seam that doesn't quite lie flat in the wash. She takes my bag firmly, the way you take a thing that could still run away.

That first night, dinner is at my grandparent’s house—eight p.m., which in Cairo means we're eating early. The whole family is there: aunts, uncles, cousins, the table crowded with bread baskets and noise. My grandfather sneezes. It's small, almost a hiccup. The table stills the way rooms do when they know the next note. Al-hamdulillah, he says.

My cousin answers first, quick as a bird: Yarhamkom Allah. My aunt follows, with yarhamkom Allah w yahdeekom. My mother, still reaching for the salt, offers her reply without looking up. Yarhamak Allah.

The blessings move around the table like current, steady and sure, each one finding its place.

I am late. Half a breath. Less than a second but the exact measure of everything I left and everything it took to come back. I feel the pause move around the table, a breeze you can't see. I say it—yarhamkom Allah. My mother puts more rice on my plate, though I'm not finished with what I have.

My grandfather, now smiling, completes the circle with his line: Yahdeena w yahdeekom. May He guide us, and guide you.

Later I climb to the roof, more for the ritual of it than the air. The city makes its night noises, none of them lonely. From here the mosques call over one another like neighbors comparing weather. I listen without answering. Some reverence happens after faith has gone quiet.

I think about what a strong body must throw out, in order to keep going. Dust, infection, air at the wrong time. Signals that once knew to travel from the mouth to another room. If the body is strong when it expels, what does it mean when it holds on?

By the end of August, I am back in Philadelphia, dragging my suitcase up the narrow stairs, the lock stiff where it always sticks. The apartment is exactly where I left it. The plant I asked a friend to water has decided to stay—green still holding, leaves uncurled, as if something had chosen not to give up on me. The cupboard still smells like cinnamon from a jar that broke in April. Small proofs that continuity is not a lie.

The first night I lie awake, still half-tuned to Cairo time, and count the sounds the room knows how to make. Heat clicking through the pipes. A siren that never arrives. My own name, said in my head the way my grandfather says it.

On my walk to class, a woman sneezes and I say “bless you” automatically. She says thank you in that flat, closed-mouth way people use when a stranger holds a door open—half habit, half obligation, already moving on. I think about how many times in a day we make space for one another without meeting. Maybe this is also a kind of blessing. Not the sharp kind. Not the old house kind. But the thin thread that keeps a morning from coming apart.

A blessing means different things depending on which wall it's asked to pass through. Some words are closed doors and some are keys. Some are the breath you push through your teeth, to remind yourself you have a mouth.

As I write this tonight, in Philadelphia, it's early November—the kind of week where the weather can't decide what it wants. The air is warm but the windows fog, and the radiator knocks like someone you're not expecting but are glad to see. I set a cup of black tea by the window and watch the street lamp cut the rain into sharp diagonals. Somewhere above me, a neighbor laughs in a language I don't speak, and I understand perfectly that the joke was good.

For a long time I thought belonging, here, meant answering correctly—that if I learned the right words, the right timing, I could make myself legible here. But maybe belonging is quieter than that. Maybe it's less about being understood and more about the willingness to speak anyway, to let both languages exist in the same breath even if no one is listening. To hold what can't be translated without trying to force it into new shapes.


It's late when I sneeze—unexpected, almost joyful. It's the kind of sneeze that surprises you into smiling. I say al-hamdulillah because the Arabic arrives first, because it still knows the way. I wait for the response without meaning to. The room does what rooms do when no one lives on the other side of the wall—it keeps its silence.

“Bless you,” I say a moment later, a second voice to meet the first. Not translation. Not replacement. Just two hands offering the same small cup.

The tea cools.

On the street, a car passes like a line drawn with the softest pencil.

The night has the manners to keep being night.
abio: Mariam ElNaggar is from Cairo, Egypt, and is a senior studying Environmental Studies and Philosophy, Politics, and Economics at the University of Pennsylvania.

title: Gramatyka
author: Zuzanna Ginczanka
poem:
(—a wrosnąć w słowa tak radośnie,
a pokochać słowa tak łatwo—
trzeba tylko wziąć je do ręki i obekrzeć jak burgund pod światło).
Przymiotniki przeciągają się jak koty
i jak koty są stworzone do pieszczot
miękkie koty ciepłe i potulne mruczą tkliwość andante i maesto.
Miękkie koty mają w oczach jeziora i ziel-topiel wodorostną na dnie.
Patrzę sennie w źrenice kocie
tajemnicje i szklane i zdradne.
Oto jest bryła i kształt, oto jest treść nieoǳowna,
konkretność istoty rzeczy, materia wkuta w rzeczownik,
i nieruchomość świata i spokój martwot i stałość,
coś, co trwa wciąż i jest, słowo stężone w ciało.
Oto są proste stoły i twarde drewniane ławy,
oto są wątłe i mokre z tkanek roślinnych trawy,
oto jest rudy kościół, co w Bogu gotykiem sterczy,
i oto jest żylne tętnicze luǳkie najprostsze serce.
Zaś przysłówek to nagły cud
niespoǳianka potartych krzesiw—
było coś nie wiadomo jak
a już teraz jest w skos i w poprzek
i oburącz oplata myśl i jest pewnie rzewnie i dobrze.
A zaimki to malutkie pokoiczki,
gǳie na oknach rosną małe doniczki.
Każdy kącik – to pamiątka po dawniej
a są tylko dla Ciebie i dla mnie.
Tu tajemną abrakadabrą
kwitną prawa miłosnych algebr:
ja—to ty, ty—to ja (równanie) 
ja bez ciebie—ty beze mnie to zero.
My lubimy otuleni zmierzchami
w małych słowach jak w szufladkach szperać.
Ja to ty—ty to ja. Równanie.
A zaimki są tak tajne jak kwiaty,
jak malutkie, malutkie pokoiczki,
w których mieszkasz w tajemnicy przed światem.
(—więc weź tylko słowo do ręki
i obejrzyj jak burgund pod światło,
a wrosnąć w słowa tak radośnie,
a pokochać słowa tak łatwo.—).
transpoem:
(—and to grow into words so joyfully,
and to love words so easily
You only have to take them in hand and gaze as if  burgundy wine under light).
Like cats, adjectives stretch
and like cats are created for caress
soft cats, warm and docile purr in tender andante and maesto.
Soft cats, have eyes of the lake, like green-melt algae in the deep.
I look sleepily into cat pupils
Transparent secrets and betrayal.                         
Here is solidity and shape, here is indispensable content,
a concrete essence of things, matter carved into noun,
and the immobility of the world and the peace of deadness and constancy,
something, that lasts and is, word condensed into flesh.
Here are simple tables and hard wooden benches,
here are the fragile wet tissues of grass,
here is the red church, as it stands in Gothic for God,
and here it is, venous and arterial, the simplest of human hearts.
Yet the adverb is a sudden miracle
the surprise of flint rubbed together—
there was something and now, we don't know how, 
 it’s diagonal and crosswise
and with both hands it embraces thought and it’s certainly tender and good.
And pronouns are tiny little rooms,
Where in windows lie small flower pots.
Every corner is a memento of the past
and they are only for you and me.
Here, in a secret abracadabra
the laws of love algebras bloom:
I—am you, you—are me (equals)
Me without you—you without me means nothing.
 Wrapped in twilights we love
to rummage in small words as in drawers.
I am you—you are me. Equals.
And pronouns are as secret as flowers,
like tiny, tiny little rooms,
where you live in secret from the world.
(—so just take a word in your hand
and look at it like the burgundy wine against the light,
and grow into words so joyfully,
and fall in love with words so easily.—).
note:
The poem "Gramatyka" is from a book of poetry called O centaurach, (or Of/About/On Centaurs). O centaurach was Zuzanna Ginczanka's first and only book of poetry, published in 1936, between the two world wars.

For the tone, "Gramatyka" definitely feels a bit more formal, but also is casual at some times, and has a very modern feel. The language is very descriptive in terms of things and settings, but it’s extremely abstract. The beginning of the poem and the end of the poem are extremely similar and are counterparts for each other, as the same lines are repeated in different orders.

Some of the phrasing feels almost personal, as if the poet is speaking to the reader, encouraging them to write and to love. Mystical and religious undertones surface throughout the poem, too, especially in lines like “something, that which lasts and is, word condensed into your body” and “here is the red church, as it stands in Gothic for God.”

This poem is basically saying: words are incredible. They allow you to express yourself and say all of the things you want to say. Words build up our language and our culture, which affects how we interact with each other and the world.
abio: Zuzanna Ginczanka was a Polish-Jewish poet of the interwar period. She was born in Kiev, Ukraine and was raised by her grandmother, who was said to be responsible for her poetic upbringing. Ginczanka began writing poems at the age of four and went on to publish her first and only book of poetry, O centaurach. She became nationally recognised for O centaurach by the time she was sixteen. Her first language was Russian, but she spoke Polish with her friends and chose to write her poems in Polish. From 1939–1942, Ginczanka lived in the city of Lviv in occupied Poland where, at the age of 22, she married the Polish-Jewish art historian Michał Weinzieher. With the Nazi invasion of Poland, the situation of the Jewish population changed dramatically for the worse. In September 1942, Ginczanka's husband decided to leave Lviv in hopes of escaping the internment. Together, they moved to Kraków where, after lots of hiding from and escaping from the Nazis, Ginczanka was arrested and killed just before the end of WWII.
tbio: Ruby Fredericks-Gzryb is a high school sophomore at Meridian Academy in Boston, MA. She is passionate about theater and enjoys the relationship between acting and reciting poetry. Fredericks-Gzryb has been glad to connect with her Polish heritage through this project and is currently preparing to compete in the "Poetry Out Loud" state semi-finals. In her free time, she plays piano and spends time with her dog, Scooby.

title: درخت ارغوان
author: Amir Houshang Ebtehaj
poem:
ارغوان شاخه همخون جدا مانده من
آسمان تو چه رنگ است امروز؟
آفتابی‌ست هوا؟
یا گرفته است هنوز؟
من در این گوشه که از دنیا بیرون است
آسمانی به سرم نیست
از بهاران خبرم نیست
آنچه می‌بینم دیوار است
آه این سخت سیاه
آنچنان نزدیک است
که چو بر می‌کشم از سینه نفس
نفسم را بر می‌گرداند
ره چنان بسته که پرواز نگه
در همین یک قدمی می‌ماند
کورسویی ز چراغی رنجور
قصه‌پرداز شب ظلمانیست
نفسم می‌گیرد
که هوا هم اینجا زندانی‌ست
هر چه با من اینجاست
رنگ رخ باخته است
آفتابی هرگز
گوشه چشمی هم
بر فراموشی این دخمه نینداخته است
اندر این گوشه خاموش فراموش شده
کز دم سردش هر شمعی خاموش شده
یاد رنگینی در خاطر من
گریه می‌انگیزد
ارغوانم آنجاست
ارغوانم تنهاست
ارغوانم دارد می‌گرید
transpoem:
Arghavan,  
my blood-bound branch, left behind.  
What color is your sky today?  
Is the air sunlit,  
or still overcast?  
Outside the world,  
in this corner—  
no sky rests above my head,  
nothing of spring I've heard.  
A wall is all I see.  
And this hard black wall—  
it looms so close.
As I push a breath up,  
it pushes my breath back down.  
So blocked is the way  
that even my gaze  
can’t move a step ahead.  
A pale light from a sickly flame,  
echoing the story of a dark night.  
My breath fails me;  
even the air here is caged.  
All that surrounds me 
has faded to pale.  
Upon the oblivion of this tomb,  
not even a glance has the sun ever spared.  
In this quiet, forgotten corner,  
where the cold breath has dimmed every flame,  
a colorful memory lingers 
and fills my eyes.  
My Arghavan—it waits there,  
alone,  
softly weeping.
note: My translation of Ebtehaj’s "The Arghavan Tree" reflects my engagement with bringing modern Iranian literary voices to English-speaking readers.
abio: Amir Houshang Ebtehaj, widely known by his pen name H. E. Sayeh (“Shadow”), was a contemporary Persian poet whose poems capture a spirit of nostalgia and longing, and often express subtle protest after the Iranian Revolution. Ebtehaj was imprisoned for several months during political crackdowns, and “The Arghavan Tree” was written during imprisonment. Although not formally exiled, increasing cultural and political restrictions led him to leave Iran in 1987, and he never returned. He passed away in 2022, leaving a lasting legacy in contemporary Persian literature.
tbio: Elahe Eizadi is an Iranian master’s student in English and Anglo-American Studies at La Sapienza University in Rome, with a particular focus on literature and translation.

title: Yedi qırımtatar aş tapmacası
author: Anonymous
poem:
10.6
Astı hasır,
Üstü hasır,
İçi ise may sasır.

10.7
Başta özüni soyğanlar,
Soñ içini oyğanlar,
Pirniçnen qarıştırıp
İçine qıyma qoyğanlar.

10.18
Qatlaması qırq qat,
Furunıña qoy, qızart.
Bal-yağ ile yaqıla –
Gülbe şeker ne acet?

10.19
Qaşıq üstünde yatam
Ayaqlarım uzatam.

10.26
Opladım, opladım,
Tos-tomalaq topladım.

10.27
Sarı suvda sandal oynay.

10.35
