Ev töpesi oyuldı,
İçindeki coyuldı.
transpoem:
10.6
A mat on the bottom,
A mat on the top,
In the space between
Fragrant fat.

10.7
First they peeled it,
Then they cored it.
A mixture of meat and rice
They put inside.

10.18
A concoction of forty layers,
Put it in the oven to bake.
Pour over it butter and honey.
Who’d then need rose jam?

10.19
I sleep on a spoon
Stretching my legs.

10.26
I jumped and skipped,
I gathered a bundle
Perfectly round.

10.27
A boat splashes around in a golden puddle.

10.35
The top of a house was scooped out,
Its residents perished.
note:
The folkloric and the avant-garde imaginations often resemble one another, as we know from the twentieth-century Eastern European poets such as Velimir Khlebnikov, Vasko Popa, and Mak Dizdar and the Americans in dialogue with Eurasian and other oral traditions such as Charles Simic and Jerome Rothenberg. The ancient can mirror the very current, even futuristic. Many riddles from anywhere in the world present the mundane as strange, causing the audience to experience delight at seeing objects, phenomena, and creatures in their midst in a new light. Crimean Tatar enigmas are no exception.

These delicate and sound-rich tiny poems present me with quite a challenge. How do I translate them without rendering them prosaic or sing-songy? They are not necessarily for children, although they possess some of the childlike wonder at the world, a quality not out of place in artistic expression generally. I could not manage to craft consistent rhymes to follow the original, but I do hope that some sonic play came through in the English by means of slant rhyme, alliteration, and assonance. It gives me some encouragement that the images – quite stunning in their compression and suggestiveness – seem to have survived the linguistic transfer.

My selection of seven enigmas constitutes a miniature Crimean Tatar feast. While Berbercan gives solutions in parenthesis after each enigma, I have decided to offer them in the note instead. (Perhaps you would want to play along. I hope you are hungry.) We have: 10.6 and 10.35 köbete (a savory phyllo pastry), 10.7 biber dolması (stuffed pepper), 10.18 baqlava, 10.19 laqşa (a lentil noodle dish), 10.26 sarma (stuffed grape leaves), and 10.27 çiberek (fried dough filled with meat). You may recognize many of these dishes from their counterparts in Eastern European, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Central Asian cuisines.
abio:
The riddles are products of a folk tradition, which means that their authors are anonymous. I have taken the originals from the Turkologist Mehmet Turgut Berbercan’s anthology Kırım Tatar Bilmeceleri(Istanbul, 2013), where they are numbered, given in the modern Crimean Tatar Latin alphabet, and translated into Turkish. Berbercan gives us as his source the germinal anthology by Şevket Asanov and Ablâziz Veliyev, Тапмаджалар(Tashkent, 1988). They cover a wide variety of subjects, from the earth and the sky, the human body, and fruits and vegetables to clothes, tools and different types of equipment, musical instruments, and even some modern technology like television sets, trains, and space shuttles.

Crimean Tatar is a West Kipchak language belonging to the larger Turkic family. UNESCO considers it endangered. It is spoken in Crimea(the Ukrainian peninsula under Russian occupation since 2014), and by diasporic communities in the surrounding region. A considerable number of speakers still lives in Uzbekistan where their ancestors had been forcibly resettled by Stalin’s regime in 1944. It has been historically written in the Perso-Arabic alphabet and nowadays in Cyrillic and Roman scripts.
tbio: Denis Ferhatović is a Bosnian-American scholar and writer. His essays, poems, reviews, translations, and co-translations have been published in Rumba under Fire, Index on Censorship, The Riddle Ages, Iberian Connections, Turkoslavia, Trinity Journal of Literary Translation (JoLT), DoubleSpeak, Asymptote, Grouchy Medievalist Substack, Ellipse Magazine, Reading in Translation, Hopscotch Translation, and Strane. His scholarly work appears in various journals and essay collections. His monograph is entitled Borrowed Objects and the Art of Poetry: Spolia in Old.

title: Een godswonder
author: Bart Chabot
poem:
ik was terug op aarde, en zulks niet tot mijn verdriet
sterker, ik was terug in den haag
waar mijn wieg had gestaan en je mijn graf kon vinden
bordjes wezen de weg

ik zat voor de verandering goed in mijn vel
dat was wel eens anders geweest
wat zou ik, teruggekeerd, kunnen doen; wat kon ik uitrichten?

terwijl ik door de binnenstad dwaalde, wierp ik af en toe
een vlugge blik in een winkelruit en zag mezelf voorbijgaan
maar het winkelend publiek, talrijk op deze koopzondag,
ontwaarde me niet, haastte zich met volle tassen vooruit
en denderde dwars door me heen
zonder dat het me een schrammetje opleverde
ik bleef, onder de voet gelopen
en vertrapt, intact
die zorg, heel blijven, uit één stuk,
kon ik met een gerust hart achter me laten

bleef de vraag: wat kon ik doen?
over water lopen had ik onder de knie
en als ik naar de noord- of zuidpool ging, om eens
iets te noemen, daar een handstand maakte
en mijn vingers losjes tegen het ijs hield,
dan draaide de aarde op mijn vijf vingertoppen om haar as
dat vergde geen bijzondere inspanning: een koud kunstje
maar zou me dat op één vingertop lukken?
ik had de benodigde diploma’s op zak
maar bezat ik ook de vereiste vaardigheden?

had ik dat huzarenstukje na enig oefenen onder de knie
dan kon ik me aan de wonderbare brood-
en wijnvermenigvuldiging wagen —
en laat dat brood bij nader inzien maar zitten
transpoem:
I returned on earth, and it didn’t make me sad,
in fact, I was back in The Hague
where my cradle had been and my grave could be found
signs were showing the way
 
I was in good shape these days
that certainly hadn’t always been the case;
upon return, what could I do, what to create?
 
straying downtown, I cast an occasional short
glance into a store window and saw myself passing by
but the shopping crowd, countless on this trading Sunday,
failed to perceive me, hastened on with full bags
and banged smack through me
without causing so much as a scratch;
knocked over and trampled
I stayed intact
that task of keeping whole, unscathed,
could be put behind me in peace of mind
 
remained the question: how to spend my time?
I’d mastered walking on the sea
and a visit to the North or South Pole, to give
one example, doing a handstand there,
putting my fingers lightly on the ice,
then the earth would rotate on my five fingertips
which took no special effort: a piece of icy cake
but would one single fingertip succeed?
I owned the right degrees
but did I also have the required skills?
 
achieving that master feat after some practising
I could take a chance at the miraculous
multiplying of bread and wine –
and on second thoughts, never mind the bread
note:
While American English generally likes more commas, Chabot’s poems have hardly any punctuation, so from the start, there was a basic challenge to this translation. However, a mild compromise — or “give and take” — now allows for the English version to fully showcase this poem’s bold beauty and original intrigue. Chabot agrees with my well-weighed additions of commas here and there, and the text is so compelling that readers will easily get used to the overall lack of punctuation.

This poem is as personal as it is universal, set in Holland’s famous international city of The Hague, Chabot’s town, where United States President John Adams bought a house. The Hague has been the world city of peace and law for 125 years, hosting the 2025 NATO summit last year. The English version of this poem is able to maintain the strength of the Dutch source material because names of important cities such as The Hague have been kept intact and authentic.

The balance between respecting the original text and rendering fluent English is always tricky. To my surprise and pleasure, Chabot himself, at one point, suggested skipping the translation of a particular phrase that in English would be “untranslatable," as any alternative would disturb the poem's coherence.
abio: Bart Chabot has been one of Holland’s most original and successful poets, novelists, biographers, and performers for the last forty-five years, winning national awards and engaging a broad audience with his sharp irony and unusual humor. Critics have praised his work as “magic, witty, accessible," with “poetic and disarming observations."
tbio: Winner of a PEN America Grant in 2021, Arno Bohlmeijer is a novelist and poet who writes in both English and Dutch and who has published in six countries – in the U.S. with Houghton Mifflin, and in the anthology Universal Oneness: Magnum Opus Poems from around the World. His novel Narrowly, about rare solidarity, will appear in September 2026.

title: शान्ति की दुकान
author: Kunwar Narain
poem:
मुँहल्ले में वह शांति बेचता है।
मंदिर-मस्जिदों की
एक दुकान है उसकी
मेरे घर से बिल्कुल लगी हुई।
सुबह सुबह मुँहअँधेरे दो घंटे
लाउडस्पीकर न बजाने के
वह मुझसे सौ रुपये महीने लेता है।
वह जानता है कि मैं
उन अभागों में से हूँ
जो शांति के बिना
जीवित नहीं रह सकते।
वह जानता है कि आनेवाली सदी में
साफ पानी और शुद्ध हवा से भी ज्यादा
शांति की किल्लत रहेगी।
वह जानता है
कि गरीब के जमाने अब लद चुके :
अब उसे अपना पेट पालने के लिए
शांति का धंधा अपनाना है।
मैं उसका आभारी हूँ।
भारत जैसे देश में
जहाँ कितने आसमान छू रही
सौ रुपये महीने की दर से
अगर दो घंटे रोज भी शांति मिल सके
तो महँगी नहीं!
transpoem:
In my neighborhood
is a shop 
with loudspeakers
next to my house

He takes a hundred rupees per month that I give him
to not turn on the loudspeakers
Early morning at the break of dawn

He knows that I am
one of the unfortunate ones
who cannot live
without peace!

He knows that for the future generations
there will be more need for peace
than clean water and clean air

He knows that
times for fighting are over
and to bring the bread home
        he must be a seller of peace

I am indebted to him
in a country like India
where inflation rates have flown sky high
for only a hundred rupees per month for two hours of peace per day
it sure is a bargain!
note:
I chose शान्ति की दुकान because I liked the concept of selling peace. The poem is also somewhat contemporary, and though I don’t live in India, I could relate to it. The poem is more positive than the poet's other poems I considered, and I didn't want to work with a depressing poem. I also wanted to pick something I thought my grandmother would like.

This poem was published in 2002, so the environment it describes for the most part still applies, today. In India (as well as many other places), many shopkeepers will play very loud music through loudspeakers in an attempt to gain attention and attract customers. It can become quite a problem in large cities, where buildings are so close together that many shops can be heard all at once, creating accumulative noise. Often, as expressed in Narain’s poem, the shops start playing music very early in the morning, which is extremely annoying to the people who live in apartments right next to or above them. शान्ति की दुकान describes the speaker’s interaction with a shopkeeper, and an agreement they have that if the speaker pays the shopkeeper 100 rupees per month, he will delay starting the music for two hours in the morning. I don’t speak Hindi, so the first thing that I observed about the poem when I saw it was that it has six stanzas, some with indentation choices that seem deliberate, and might be used to connect ideas between lines. The number of lines vary from stanza to stanza, but the poem has an obvious pattern, with one exception at the end. The line numbers are as follows: 4, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5.

When I met with my translation mentor, Achla B. Madan, my grandmother, she told me quite a lot about the poem. She often didn’t have very many answers for any of the specific analytical questions, but when she simply told me her thoughts on the poem, I frantically took notes. Those notes are most of what guided me through my translating process. She also gave me her literal translation (I say that it’s hers because I don’t speak Hindi, so she did the translating part), and that gave me a better idea of the content of the poem. Another interesting thing about my grandmother’s translation is that she speaks and writes in proper English, but she included a few more informal phrases, such as “it sure is a bargain.”

My grandmother told me that the wording used in the poem was fairly casual; in her words, the diction of the poem is “what you would use in your common talk.” In my first translation, I chose to embrace this aspect of the poem. In her literal translation, my grandmother wrote “to fulfill his daily needs” --which is, in fact, not entirely literal. A literal translation of this phrase, in Hindi, would be “to fill his stomach,” but it is an idiom that means “to fulfill his daily needs.” Logically, the daily need that selling peace fulfills is earning money. Keeping my informal writing theme, I translated this as “to bring the bread home.”

For my second translation, my focus was to do the opposite, and use flowery language to paint a picture, in part of the scene of the shop, but mostly create the imagery of the chaotic life of the speaker and the reasons behind why peace is necessary. I think that the original poem does both these things, and I wanted to continue and even give the poem more of this. I used many of the words and phrases that my grandmother gave me initially, such as “it abuts my house” and “the need for peace will supersede.” Some of the lines that I added include “he must undertake” and “inflation rates have grown immensely.”
abio:
Kunwar Narain (often spelled Kunwar Narayan) was an Indian poet who lived from 1927 to 2017 and whose poems are some of the most popular works of Hindi poetry. Many of his works include very deep messages, often relating to death, as he was a “meditative poet" (Subramaniam). He was born in Uttar Pradesh, a state in the northern part of India, and he had quite a tragic childhood. When he was eleven, both his mother and sister died of tuberculosis. This contributed to the recurring metaphors around death in his poetry.

In 1993, he wrote "A Shop That Sells Peace."
tbio: Apollo Ravi Constantine is a tenth grader at Meridian Academy in Boston. He enjoys mountain biking and BMX, as well as playing the trumpet and guitar, and composing music.

title: سلام!
author: Seyed Ali Salehi
poem:
سلام!
حال همه‌ی ما خوب است
ملالی نيست جز گم شدنِ گاه به گاهِ خيالی دور،
که مردم به آن شادمانیِ بی‌سبب می‌گويند
با اين همه عمری اگر باقی بود
طوری از کنارِ زندگی می‌گذرم
که نه زانویِ آهویِ بی‌جفت بلرزد و
نه اين دلِ ناماندگارِ بی‌درمان!
تا يادم نرفته است بنويسم
حوالیِ خوابهای ما سالِ پربارانی بود
می‌دانم هميشه حياط آنجا پر از هوای تازه‌ی باز نيامدن است
اما تو لااقل، حتی هر وهله، گاهی، هر از گاهی
ببين انعکاس تبسم رويا
شبيه شمايل شقايق نيست!
راستی خبرت بدهم
خواب ديده‌ام خانه‌ئی خريده‌ام
بی‌پرده، بی‌پنجره، بی‌در، بی‌ديوار … هی بخند!
بی‌پرده بگويمت
چيزی نمانده است، من چهل ساله خواهم شد
فردا را به فال نيک خواهم گرفت
دارد همين لحظه
يک فوج کبوتر سپيد
از فرازِ کوچه‌ی ما می‌گذرد
باد بوی نامهای کسان من می‌دهد
يادت می‌آيد رفته بودی
خبر از آرامش آسمان بياوری!؟
نه ری‌را جان
نامه‌ام بايد کوتاه باشد
ساده باشد
بی حرفی از ابهام و آينه،
از نو برايت می‌نويسم
حال همه‌ی ما خوب است
اما تو باور نکن!
transpoem:
Hello.
We are all okay.
Nothing’s wrong here
beyond the occasional wandering off
of that murky dream
which people call Unreasonable Happiness.
Regardless, if I have time left
I’ll live without hurting a deer
or paining this shaky, incurable heart.
Let me write, before I forget,
how rainy it was for our dreams this year
and I know your courtyard,
wherever it may be, always blooms
with the scent of not coming back,
but at least occasionally make note
that a smile in a dream while sleeping
isn’t the same as the face of an anemone.
I should tell you… I dreamed I bought a house
without curtains, or windows, or doors, or walls—
Oh, keep laughing!
But let me be honest:
there isn’t much time left. I’ll be forty soon
and I believe the fact that tomorrow will come
is a good omen.
In this moment, a platoon of white doves
is flying above our courtyard
and wind carries the scent
of the names of my beloveds.
Do you remember leaving home
to bring back news
of the sky's tranquility?
No, Rira dear—
this letter must be brief,
simple—
without doubts or any words
to cause a ripple.
Let me start over:
We are all okay, but
don't believe me.
note:
I have always been interested in the image that this poem presents; as a conversational poem in the form of a letter written to a loved one, the one-sided conversation feels like talking into the void and expecting a response. The speaker reminisces about the past and fantasizes about the future, sharing their dreams, despair, and sense of hope.

One of the difficulties of translation was finding English versions of certain Farsi words with many variations. For example, the English translation of the poem uses the word "dream" throughout. In the Farsi version, nearly every mention of "dream" is actually written using a different word. These Farsi words are not necessarily equivalent to the ones used in the English translation. In one instance, the Farsi poem uses a word that discusses delusion, but I chose to translate this word to "murky dream" because Salehi is using the Farsi word in a more positive tone than the English "delusion." Then, later, in the line: "how rainy it was for our dreams this year," the Farsi word directly translates to sleep, but the word "sleep" doesn't fully evoke the meaning of the line, so again I replaced it with "dream."

Another instance of this translation by interpretation was for the line: "but at least occasionally make note." In the Farsi version, the poet uses several words in close succession that convey a similar meaning but with slightly different direct translations. Salehi writes وهله، گاهی، هر از گاهی, which directly translates to "moment, every once in a while, and sometimes." The final translation conveys the meaning of all three phrases appropriately by using the English word “occasionally,” keeping true to the main idea in the Farsi version.
abio: One of Iran’s most prominent contemporary poets, is Seyed Ali Salehi, although he is currently living in Tehran, he was Born in 1955 in a small town in south west of Iran. He first published the majority of his works in small literary gatherings and local newspapers in 1970s and by nineteen, he was awarded the Forough literary Prize. From 2001 to 2003 he was the chairman of the Writers Union although he was constantly interrogated due to his literary and political protests. He was also the editor of various literary magazines such as the literary magazine Sokhan, a magazine that’s been banned from publication since 2000, and the editor of the magazine Literarischer.
tbio: With encouragement from her parents, Sogand Shenavar began studying English at the age of nine and continued throughout college, where she majored in English language and literature. She is currently completing her masters in English and Anglo-American studies at La Sapienza University in Rome.

title: Pharsalia. 7.617-637.
author: Lucan
poem:
inpendisse pudet lacrimas in funere mundi
mortibus innumeris, ac singula fata sequentem
quaerere letiferum per cuius uiscera uolnus
exierit, quis fusa solo uitalia calcet, 620
ore quis aduerso demissum faucibus ensem
expulerit moriens anima, quis corruat ictus,
quis steterit dum membra cadunt, qui pectore tela
transmittant aut quos campis adfixerit hasta,
quis cruor emissis perruperit aera uenis 625
inque hostis cadat arma sui, quis pectora fratris
caedat et, ut notum possit spoliare cadauer,
abscisum longe mittat caput, ora parentis
quis laceret nimiaque probet spectantibus ira
quem iugulat non esse patrem. mors nulla querella 630
digna sua est, nullosque hominum lugere uacamus.
non istas habuit pugnae Pharsalia partes
quas aliae clades: illic per fata uirorum,
per populos hic Roma perit; quod militis illic,
mors hic gentis erat: sanguis ibi fluxit Achaeus, 635
Ponticus, Assyrius; cunctos haerere cruores
Romanus campisque uetat consistere torrens.
transpoem:
It shames me to have wasted tears on countless deaths
While the world attends her funeral,
And to ask, as I trace individual fates,
Through whose insides the fatal wound went,
Who tramples the vitals levelled to the earth,
Who releases the buried sword from their throat
With their final breath,
Who stumbles at the blow,
Who wavers while their limbs fall,
Who endures arrows in their chest
Or is ploughed by a spear into the plains?
Whose blood from whose veins slices the air,
Falling onto their enemy’s weapons,
Who mangles their brother’s chest
And so not to know the corpse they pick at,
Sends the severed head afar,
Who torments their parent’s face,
Proving by their weight of anger to those watching
That they murder not a father?

No death is worthy of its own lament,
I leave no time to grieve individuals.
Pharsalia is not like other disasters:
There, Rome perished by her men,
Here by her people.
There it was a soldier’s death,
Here, a nation’s loss.
There, Achaea, Pontus, Assyria let their blood:
The Roman flood forbade all other kinds

To cling to the fields and settle.
note: In my translation I hoped to heighten the uneasy effect created by Lucan’s empty questioning through placing the question words at the beginning of each line. Instead of the glory (κλέος) offered by the Homeric poeticising of deaths in the much earlier Greek Iliad, I wanted to promote Lucan’s dishonourable portrayal of the death of men in civil war. One word that particularly interested me was spoliare in the way that it suggested the greed of those desiring to plunder their victim’s corpses: I translated this as "pick at", hoping to evoke the image of a bird of prey mincing its carrion. The dead bodies are no longer loved ones or even humans, but flesh to be profited from. All the dead are equal in battle, but even more so from the fact that it is self-same slaughter in this war. I somewhat had a more difficult decision to make through the wording to describe the wounding of the men in the opening lines. The Latin is explicitly alliterative (uiscera uolnus...uitalia), made possible through the jumbling of word order allowed in the language. In an English rendering, ‘viscera’ and ‘vitals’ are certainly possible translations, but at the risk of sounding archaic. I opted for the semi-alliterative effect of ‘wound’ (volnus) and ‘vitals’ (vitalia) as a compromise. On a structural note, I separated the final section of Latin into its own paragraph, as it seemed to mark a change tone after the indirect questions. The poet returns cyclically to his original statement that no death deserves its own record when Rome herself is dying. Now that he has evoked individual – if nameless deaths - this assertion appears to be somewhat contradictory. Although Lucan wants to lament only the death of Rome, he can only do this by lamenting its men.
abio: This translation is taken as an extract from Lucan’s epic poem Pharsalia, which charts the conflict between Julius Caesar and his rival Pompey. Lucan was a Roman author writing under Nero and he experienced firsthand the vagaries of an emperor’s favour. The fluctuations of despair and renewal are what makes his poem so engaging, and likewise his nuanced portrayal of both sides of the civil war. This extract is taken from the culminating battle scene in Thessaly, northern Greece, and is vehement in deglamourizing a civil conflict. I picked this passage from the ten books of Pharsalia as it felt most applicable to the context of modern civil war and the role of a poet in commemorating their nation’s suffering. It also reads as a poem within a poem in the way that Lucan sets out his aim and then offers a stream of unanswered questions, which both individuate and generalize the deaths they record. No name is given to the men who die, and I would argue that this is a conscious act of defamation from his disgust at the perversion of civil war. Just as the men he writes of depersonalize those who are closest to them, so too does Lucan make their deaths anonymous.
tbio: Nell Gardiner is an exchange student at the University of Pennsylvania from Trinity College in Dublin, Ireland. She studies classics while making art on the side, and she likes Philadelphia and its strange traditions very much.

title: Catullus 101
author: Catullus
poem:
Multas per gentes et multa per aequora vectus 
     advenio has miseras, frater, ad inferias, 
ut te postremo donarem munere mortis      
      et mutam nequiquam alloquerer cinerem. 
quandoquidem fortuna mihi tete abstulit ipsum. 
     heu miser indigne frater adempte mihi, 
nunc tamen interea haec, prisco quae more parentum 
     tradita sunt tristi munere ad inferias, 
accipe fraterno multum manantia fletu,      
atque in perpetuum, frater, ave atque vale.
transpoem:
Now I have come through many peopled lands, 
By many seas to serve these wretchèd rites 
My brother! so that I could offer you Death’s decorations.  
You are dead, and I have come 
To speak at your unspeaking ashes. Why? 
 
That Goddess, Fate, has stolen you from me 
O brother, undeservedly from me -  
 
But…however…now… now take them! Take your rites! 
These fossilized rites our fathers handed us  
This sad and pitiful service to the tomb… 
 
God, it’s all soaked now with your brother’s tears.   
 
Brother! always, ‘hail thee, and…’  goodbye.
note: This poem is an elegy for the poet's brother, who has died far away from Rome. It differs starkly in tone from the rest of Catullus's corpus, and masterfully and tragically explores the vacuum left by a loved one's passing, and the futility of funeral rites to truly reconcile this grief and to service the dead. It has been my intention to display the futility, as many translators have not focused on rendering this powerful, human aspect of the mythologized poem by way of employing an idiomatic, personal attitude. For instance, I have added the English exhortation "God" to the line accipe fraterno multum manantia fletu – literally “Take [these rites] laden with many fraternal tears” – or I have broken the mostly pentametric translation (keeping in line with Catullus’s formal poem) to demonstrate the author’s overwhelming emotion in “Death’s decorations. / You are dead, and I have come”. Regarding my unorthodox punctuation, I have chosen to render the stacking of adverbs in nunc tamen interea – literally “now however meanwhile” – as a grief-filled loss of composure. Moreover, I have rendered frater, ave atque vale – literally “Brother, hail and be strong” – which some scholars believe was a sort of stock phrase in funeral rites, as another instance of Catullus going through the motions of the rites, only for these motions to finally break. This differs from the traditional translation of a formal sendoff, which I do not believe matches the tone of the rest of the poem.
abio: Catullus ( 84 – c. 54 BC) was a Roman lyric poet whose often personal and humorous poems expound upon topics of love (particularly his obsession with a woman he calls Lesbia), poetry, and daily life.
tbio: Jax Gottschalch is a freshman at the University of Pennsylvania, studying classics and physics. He translates Latin, Greek, and Danish poetry into English verse. He also composes verse in Greek and Latin.
